title: Threat modelling and security boundaries
problem: Security reviews that start from a checklist miss the attacks that matter for this system, and reviews that start from fear never finish.
summary: Threat modelling draws the system as a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries, applies STRIDE and abuse cases at each one, and answers with layers: zero-trust identity and authorisation inside the network, segmentation to cut blast radius, and DDoS absorbed at the edge first.
catTip: I threat-model the house daily: front door, cat flap, the window the humans forget. For each I ask who could get in, what they could take, and whether anyone would notice. Then I nap in the safest spot.

recall.q: Apply STRIDE to the boundary between your services and the database when every service connects with the same password. Name two threats and their fixes.
recall.a: Spoofing: anyone holding the password is any service, fixed by per-workload identities (mTLS or dynamic credentials). Repudiation: the audit log shows one user for everything, fixed by per-service credentials. A third is elevation of privilege through injection into an over-privileged account, fixed by least-privilege grants and parameterised queries.

guide.breaks: Without a model you defend the parts you happen to know about, trust the private network because it is private, and discover the abuse case when the ticket bots or the scrapers do.
guide.tradeoffs: Modelling takes time from building and goes stale as the architecture changes, zero trust adds identity and policy machinery to every internal call, and edge DDoS protection is a cost paid before any attack happens.
guide.explainSimply: Threat modelling is walking round the house with a burglar's eyes: list every door and window, and at each one ask who could pretend to be the postman, swap the parcel, sneak a look in, block the door or reach the safe. Then fix the worst ones first, and walk again after every renovation.
guide.hint: Who could pretend to be a service, and who would the log blame?

meow: Front door, cat flap, forgotten window: who gets in, what do they take, who notices? Model done, nap begins.

quiz.prompt: In STRIDE, which category is violated when a user deletes a post and the system has no log that could prove who did it?
quiz.explanation: Repudiation is denying an action without the system being able to prove otherwise; audit logs with request ids are the mitigation. Spoofing is about using someone else's identity, not about missing evidence.

quiz.prompt: A terabit-scale volumetric DDoS hits your API. Which layer must absorb it, and why?
options: The application servers, by autoscaling until the attack ends
The API gateway's rate limiter, keyed by client IP
An anycast CDN or edge network, because only the edge has capacity near the traffic's sources
The database, by rejecting connections above a threshold
quiz.explanation: Floods must be stopped where there is matching capacity, and anycast spreads attack traffic across many sites close to where it originates. Rate limiting and load shedding protect the gateway and services from what reaches them, not from terabits.

cards.q: List the six STRIDE threats with the property each one violates.
cards.a: Spoofing: authentication. Tampering: integrity. Repudiation: non-repudiation. Information disclosure: confidentiality. Denial of service: availability. Elevation of privilege: authorisation.

cards.q: Zero trust says the network is compromised. Does that make network segmentation pointless? Explain.
cards.a: No. Zero trust stops you relying on network location as proof of identity, so every internal call is authenticated and authorised. Segmentation still limits blast radius: a database reachable only from the application tier means a compromised edge host cannot even try the password.

glossary.full: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege
glossary.note: Microsoft's six threat categories, each the violation of one security property; applied per trust boundary or per element.
